questions.stem: A bacterial culture is treated with a drug that completely inhibits DNA gyrase, a topoisomerase. Helicase and DNA polymerase are unaffected, and replication was already under way at several forks when the drug was added. Which outcome is expected?
options: Replication continues at normal speed, because topoisomerase acts only at the very end of replication to link the two daughter molecules.
Replication forks stall shortly after drug addition, because unwinding by helicase leaves the unreplicated DNA ahead of each fork increasingly overwound and torsionally strained.
Helicase can no longer separate the two strands, because topoisomerase is the enzyme that breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.
Okazaki fragments accumulate on the lagging strand, because topoisomerase normally seals the nicks between adjacent fragments.
The separated parental strands cannot act as templates, because topoisomerase proofreads newly synthesized DNA.
questions.exp: Topoisomerase relieves the positive supercoiling that builds up ahead of a moving fork; without it the torsional strain rapidly blocks helicase, so forks stall even though helicase and polymerase themselves are intact. The Okazaki option describes the job of DNA ligase, which seals nicks between fragments and is a different enzyme.

questions.stem: In a temperature-sensitive bacterial mutant shifted to the restrictive temperature, DNA ligase is inactive while helicase, primase and DNA polymerase still function normally. Which observation is expected in cells that were replicating at the time of the shift?
options: The lagging strand remains as a series of separate Okazaki fragments, because the nicks between adjacent fragments are not sealed.
The leading strand also remains in fragments, because ligase normally cuts the leading strand into pieces during replication.
Helicase stops unwinding the parental double helix, because the torsional stress generated by unwinding can only be resolved by ligase.
No new Okazaki fragments are synthesized at all, because the synthesis of each fragment requires ligase.
RNA primers are no longer removed from the fragments, because primer removal is carried out by DNA ligase.
questions.exp: Primase and polymerase make each Okazaki fragment, so fragments still form at the restrictive temperature; ligase only forms the final phosphodiester bond between adjacent fragments, so the lagging strand stays discontinuous. The helicase option assigns ligase the torsion-relieving role that belongs to topoisomerase.

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic species, nucleosomes are arranged with a repeat length of 200 bp of DNA per nucleosome. Each nucleosome core particle contains two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, with 147 bp of DNA wrapped around the octamer. A linear stretch of this chromatin is 24,000 bp long. How many molecules of histone H3 are present in its nucleosome core particles?
options: 60 molecules
120 molecules
240 molecules
480 molecules
960 molecules
questions.exp: The stretch holds 24000 / 200 = 120 core particles, and each core particle contains two H3 molecules, giving 2 x 120 = 240. The 480 option counts all four core histone types as if each contributed H3, and the 960 option counts every protein in the octamer as H3.

questions.stem: Which statement about histones is correct?
options: Histones are acidic proteins that bind DNA through attraction between their negatively charged side chains and the positively charged DNA backbone.
Histones are covalently joined to DNA by a ligation reaction, which is what holds each nucleosome together.
Bacterial chromosomes are organized around histone octamers in the same way as eukaryotic chromosomes.
Histones are small basic proteins whose positive charges bind the negatively charged phosphate groups of the DNA backbone.
Each nucleosome core particle contains eight different histone types, one molecule of each kind.
questions.exp: Histones are rich in lysine and arginine, so they are basic and bind the acidic phosphate backbone mainly through ionic interactions, not covalent bonds. The acidic-protein option reverses the charge logic: acidic side chains would repel the DNA phosphates rather than attract them.

questions.stem: Bacteria are grown for many generations in a medium whose only nitrogen source is the heavy isotope 15N, so that all their DNA is fully heavy. The culture is then transferred to ordinary 14N medium and allowed to complete three further rounds of replication. Assuming semiconservative replication, what fraction of the double-stranded DNA molecules present at the end contain 15N in at least one of their strands?
questions.exp: The two original heavy strands never disappear: in every generation each sits in exactly one hybrid molecule, so there are always 2 molecules containing 15N, while the total number of molecules doubles each round. After three rounds there are 8 molecules, so the fraction is 2/8 = 1/4; the answer 3/4 is the fraction that is entirely new instead.

questions.stem: In a Meselson-Stahl type experiment, bacteria grown in 15N medium are shifted to 14N medium and allowed to replicate for exactly two rounds. Centrifugation then separates the DNA into two distinct bands: one at intermediate density and one fully light, with no heavy band anywhere in the tube. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Semiconservative replication is excluded, because it predicts a single intermediate band after two rounds.
Only the conservative model is excluded, because the dispersive model still predicts two separate bands.
Only the dispersive model is excluded, because the conservative model still predicts an intermediate band.
Both the conservative and the dispersive models are excluded, which is the classic evidence for semiconservative replication.
The experiment is uninterpretable, because no model predicts a light band after only two rounds.
questions.exp: After two rounds semiconservative replication gives half hybrid molecules (the intermediate band) and half fully light molecules (the light band). The conservative model would still show a fully heavy band, and the dispersive model would give one single band of uniform intermediate density, so two bands with no heavy band rule out both rivals at once.

questions.stem: Which statement about the eukaryotic (80S) ribosome is correct?
options: Its large and small subunits are assembled in the nucleolus and are exported separately to the cytoplasm, where they combine only when translation begins.
The complete 80S particle is assembled in the cytoplasm on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
It is built from a 50S large subunit and a 30S small subunit, as is the case in all living cells.
One of its subunits is made of protein only and the other of RNA only.
Its subunits are assembled in the Golgi apparatus and delivered to the cytoplasm inside transport vesicles.
questions.exp: Ribosomal RNA is transcribed and the subunits begin assembling in the nucleolus; the mature 60S and 40S subunits are then exported separately and only associate on an mRNA at initiation. The 50S plus 30S option describes the prokaryotic 70S ribosome, not the eukaryotic one.
questions.topic: Biology · eukaryotic ribosome structure and assembly

questions.stem: A eukaryotic gene consists of two exons separated by one intron, and that intron contains a stop codon in the reading frame. The DNA of the gene, intron included, is inserted into a bacterium under the control of a bacterial promoter, transcribed and translated. Which outcome is expected?
options: The normal-length protein is produced, because bacteria remove introns from RNA using the same spliceosome as eukaryotes.
No polypeptide is produced, because a bacterial ribosome cannot translate a transcript that contains intron sequences.
A protein longer than the normal one is produced, because the entire intron is translated in addition to both exons.
The normal protein is produced, with the amino acids encoded by the intron simply inserted between the two exons.
A shortened polypeptide is produced, because translation stops at the stop codon inside the intron, before the second exon is ever reached.
questions.exp: Prokaryotes generally lack spliceosomes, so the transcript keeps the intron; the ribosome translates exon 1 into the intron and terminates at the in-frame stop codon there, giving a truncated polypeptide that lacks the second exon. The inserted-amino-acids option fails because translation halts inside the intron at that stop codon rather than continuing into exon 2.

questions.stem: Which statement about RNA splicing is correct?
options: Splicing removes the exons and joins the introns together to build the mature mRNA that is translated.
Splicing takes place in the cytoplasm, on the ribosome, immediately before translation begins.
In eukaryotes, introns are removed and exons joined before the mature mRNA leaves the nucleus, whereas most bacterial genes contain no introns and their transcripts are not spliced.
Bacterial mRNAs must be spliced before translation, because bacterial genes are normally rich in introns.
Splicing alters the nucleotide sequence of the exons so that they come to encode different amino acids.
questions.exp: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is spliced in the nucleus before export, and bacterial genes are typically intron-free, so no splicing step exists in bacteria. The first option reverses the two elements: splicing removes introns and joins exons, and it does not change exon sequence.

questions.stem: A codon table shows that CAG codes for glutamine and that UAG is a stop codon. In an mRNA molecule, the codon CAG is changed to UAG by a single base substitution. This mutation is best classified as:
options: A nonsense mutation.
A missense mutation.
A silent mutation.
A frameshift mutation.
An insertion mutation.
questions.exp: The change turns a glutamine codon into a stop signal, so translation ends prematurely and a truncated polypeptide results, which is the definition of a nonsense mutation. A missense classification would require the new codon to specify a different amino acid, and a single base substitution cannot shift the reading frame.

questions.stem: The beginning of an mRNA reads AUG CCU GGU UGA, where UGA is the fourth codon and is a stop signal. Given the code AUG = methionine, CCU = proline, GGU = glycine, ACC = threonine, UGG = tryptophan, UUG = leucine, a mutation inserts one extra nucleotide, A, immediately after the first codon. Which statement is correct?
options: Only one amino acid changes, because the ribosome re-establishes the original reading frame after a single inserted nucleotide.
Methionine is still the first amino acid, but proline, glycine and every later position change, and the original UGA stop signal is never read because it is split across the new codon boundaries.
The protein becomes just methionine followed by threonine, because the new codon ACC acts as a stop signal.
The insertion is silent, because adding a single nucleotide leaves each existing codon intact.
Translation now ends at the position of the former UGA codon, but the amino acids before that point are all unchanged.
questions.exp: Inserting one nucleotide shifts every downstream group of three bases: the new codons are ACC, UGG, UUG, so proline and glycine are replaced by threonine and tryptophan, and the old UGA stop is consumed inside new codons and never read as a stop. The claim that the ribosome restores the frame misses the defining feature of a frameshift: the one-base offset persists to the end of the message.

questions.stem: A codon table gives: GAA and GAG both code for glutamate, GUA codes for valine, and UAA is a stop codon. In the same gene in two different individuals, single-base substitutions occur at the same codon: in mutant X the codon GAA becomes GAG, and in mutant Y the codon GAA becomes GUA. Which classification is correct?
options: X is a missense mutation and Y is a silent mutation.
X is a nonsense mutation and Y is a missense mutation.
X is a silent mutation and Y is a nonsense mutation.
X is a silent mutation and Y is a missense mutation.
X is a frameshift mutation and Y is a missense mutation.
questions.exp: In X the codon still specifies glutamate, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged and the mutation is silent; in Y glutamate is replaced by valine, a different amino acid, so it is missense. The nonsense option is wrong because replacing an acidic residue is not a stop signal: a nonsense mutation needs the codon itself to become a stop codon such as UAA.

questions.stem: A researcher sets up a PCR containing the DNA template, Taq polymerase and all four dNTPs, but accidentally omits the primers. The thermal cycler still runs its full programme of denaturation, annealing and extension. Which outcome is expected?
options: Amplification occurs but more slowly, because Taq polymerase is able to start synthesis on a single-stranded template without a primer.
The dNTPs anneal to the template in place of the missing primers and allow amplification to proceed.
The reaction fails because Taq polymerase is destroyed at the annealing temperature of the cycle.
One copy of the template is produced in each cycle, so the DNA accumulates linearly instead of exponentially.
No amplification occurs, because DNA polymerase cannot start a new strand and can only extend from the free 3' end that a paired primer provides.
questions.exp: Taq polymerase is thermostable but can only add nucleotides to an existing strand, so without oligonucleotide primers supplying a paired 3' end there is no extension step and no product ever accumulates. The linear-accumulation option wrongly assumes that synthesis can begin on a bare single-stranded template.
questions.topic: Biology · PCR components (primers and Taq polymerase)
questions.syl: 3. Biology: Biotechnologies (recombinant DNA technology and its applications)

questions.stem: A PCR tube starts with exactly one double-stranded DNA molecule. The reaction runs three complete cycles, and in every cycle each single strand present serves as the template for one newly synthesized complementary strand. After the third cycle, how many of the double-stranded molecules consist of two newly synthesized strands, with no original template strand at all?
options: 0 molecules
2 molecules
4 molecules
6 molecules
8 molecules
questions.exp: After cycle 1 there are 2 molecules, both hybrids of one old and one new strand; after cycle 2 there are 4 molecules, of which 2 are entirely new; after cycle 3 there are 8 molecules, and only the two strands of the original template still sit in hybrid molecules, leaving 8 - 2 = 6 that are entirely new. The 8 option forgets that each original strand persists in one hybrid molecule forever.
questions.syl: 3. Biology: Biotechnologies (recombinant DNA technology and its applications)
